prompt: Tick every true statement about IP and MAC addresses.
hint: One of the two describes where the machine is; the other, which machine it is. Take the laptop to another network and see which of the two changes.

choices.text: The IP changes when the machine connects to another network.
choices.why: The IP describes a position, like a postal address.

choices.text: The MAC travels with the equipment wherever it goes.
choices.why: The MAC is the card's identity, burned into it.

choices.text: Ranges like `192.168.x.x` are reused inside every local network and do not exist on the internet.
choices.why: They are private ranges; the router translates to the public IP through NAT.

choices.text: A website's server sees the MAC address of the laptop that visited it.
choices.why: A MAC only means anything on the local link: the server sees the MAC of the last router on its own path.

choices.text: IPv6 exists to give more speed than IPv4.
choices.why: It exists because IPv4's 4.3 billion addresses ran out — it is a question of space, not of speed.

prompt: On a public network, a machine answers ARP questions posing as the router and starts receiving its neighbours' traffic. What makes this attack possible?
hint: What does the protocol do when two machines answer the same question? Does it check anything before believing?

choices.text: ARP does not authenticate the answers: whoever answers is believed, and the answer sits in a cache for a few minutes.
choices.why: It is why HTTPS on a public network stops being a recommendation and becomes a necessity.

choices.text: ARP transmits the answers unencrypted, so they can be read and altered in transit.
choices.why: Reading is not the problem here: the attack works because the forged answer is accepted, not because the true one was read.

choices.text: The ARP cache never expires, so a forged answer is good for ever.
choices.why: The cache expires within minutes — the attacker has to repeat the answer, and that does not prevent the attack.

choices.text: ARP uses IP addresses instead of MAC ones, and so cannot tell machines on the same network apart.
choices.why: ARP does exactly the bridging between the two: it asks by IP and receives a MAC.
